lead: One harsh comment can stick in your head longer than ten kind ones.
when: When you can't shake off criticism for a long time, remember only the parts of the day that went wrong, or write off your whole effort because of one bad review, it's a good tool to reach for.
body:
You post an article. Ten people say it helped, and one says it's terrible. What you keep replaying before bed is usually that one "terrible." This tendency to be more sensitive to negative information, and to remember it more, is called negativity bias. It helps us notice threats, but it can also push our overall judgment too far.

Negativity bias refers to the tendency of negative events or information to have a greater effect on attention, memory, and evaluation than comparable positive information.

The problem isn't that you're "too sensitive," and the fix isn't forcing yourself to be positive. It's that the way your mind divides its attention may not match the real proportions. Bad news should of course be dealt with, but dealing with one problem and judging the whole thing a failure can be kept separate.
example:
In a work presentation, you hit most of your goals and missed only one formatting detail. After your manager points out the mistake, all that's left in your head is "I did a terrible job," and you're still replaying that one minute at home.

You can start by writing down the full facts: what you finished, what you missed, how big the consequences are, and how to avoid it next time. The formatting error needs fixing, but there's no need to erase everything you carefully completed. That makes your review fairer and makes it easier to improve, instead of growing more afraid of handing anything in the more you think about it.
extra: After a trip, you might remember only the long wait in line at the very end, which can make you forget that the first two days were a lot of fun. Writing a few lines about the whole trip alongside your photos can sometimes help your memory regain a sense of proportion.
steps: Write down the positive, negative, and ordinary outcomes, and fill in the whole picture first.
Ask how much the problem actually matters, not just how bad it makes you feel.
Give it one concrete action to deal with it, and once that's done, let your attention move on.
caution: Not every negative comment should be met with "just let it go." Serious risks, harm, and well-founded complaints need to be taken seriously. What you're adjusting is your overall judgment, not suppressing real problems.
exercise: Tonight, write three lines: one thing that went well today, one that didn't, and one adjustment you can make tomorrow. Don't dress it up. Just get the full information down.
brief: A few negatives grab attention: a ring of many friendly, wordless thumbs-up cards with one brick-red broken icon; a stick figure's magnifying glass is aimed only at that one negative card, its shadow enlarging it, while all the other positive information remains fully visible.
